title: Round 7: Defend an architecture decision and discuss rejected alternatives
description: Practice explaining why you chose one architecture over another, and how you communicate trade-offs to stakeholders and teammates.

data.text: Senior engineers do not just make decisions; they defend them under pressure. The interviewer asks you to pick an architecture decision from your past, explain why you made it, and describe the alternatives you rejected. The goal is to reveal your reasoning depth, not your ego.

items: State the decision in one sentence: 'We chose to store session state in Redis instead of in-memory cookies.'
List the constraints: team size, traffic volume, compliance requirements, and existing infrastructure.
Explain the chosen approach: what it does, why it fits the constraints, and how it performs in production.
Discuss the trade-offs: what you gave up and how you mitigated the downsides.
Describe the outcome: what happened after the decision was implemented.

terms.definition: A short document that captures an important architecture decision, its context, and its consequences.
A boundary within a domain where a particular model is defined and applicable, from domain-driven design.
The implied cost of future rework caused by choosing an easy or limited solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer.
A decision where gaining one quality causes losing another. Architecture is the art of balancing trade-offs.

data.text: A common trap is to defend the chosen approach while trashing the rejected alternatives. The interviewer wants to see that you evaluated the alternatives fairly and chose based on context, not bias.

data.title: Decision example
data.content: Example: choosing between a monolithic repository and a microservice architecture for a new product team.
data.code:
Decision: Start with a modular monolith.

Constraints:
- Five engineers, six-month runway to first revenue
- Compliance requirement for data locality
- Unknown product-market fit

Rejected alternatives:
- Full microservices: too many deployment and operational concerns for a small team.
- Single shared library across multiple apps: creates coupling and slows iteration.

Mitigation: Defined module boundaries with internal NuGet packages so splitting into services later is mechanical.

items: Name the alternative honestly and describe its strengths.
Explain why those strengths did not outweigh the weaknesses in your context.
Show what would need to change for that alternative to become the right choice later.
Avoid language that sounds like you are dismissing the idea out of hand.

data.text: Architecture decisions affect more than engineers. A good senior engineer can explain trade-offs to a product manager in terms of delivery speed, risk, and cost. Instead of saying 'we need a message queue,' say 'adding a message queue lets us decouple payment from fulfillment, so a shipping API outage will not block checkout. The cost is an extra infrastructure component and eventual consistency for order status.'

cards.title: Architecture Decision Records
cards.description: Short markdown files stored alongside the codebase.
cons: Can become outdated if not enforced

cards.title: Decision logs in wikis
cards.description: Centralized documentation in Confluence, Notion, or similar.
cons: Harder to enforce link to PR

cards.title: Code comments and README
cards.description: Inline comments and architecture README files.

data.title: Show the evolution
data.text: If the decision was later revisited and changed, say so. 'We started with Redis sessions, but after the team grew to twelve engineers and we adopted container orchestration, we moved to a stateless JWT approach.' That narrative proves you learn from outcomes.

data.caption: Architecture Decision Record lifecycle from proposal to outcome
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Propose ADR] --> B[Team review]
    B --> C{Accepted?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Implement]
    C -->|No| E[Reject with rationale]
    D --> F[Link ADR to PR]
    F --> G[Ship and monitor]
    G --> H[Record outcome after N months]
    H --> I[Update or supersede ADR]

data.title: Write an ADR for a recent decision
data.description: Think of a small architecture or tooling decision you made in the last month. Write a one-page ADR covering context, options, decision, and consequences.
steps: Pick a decision with at least two realistic alternatives
Write the context and constraints in three bullet points
List the options with pros and cons
Describe the consequences and how you will validate the outcome
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a concise, honest document that a future team member could read to understand why the system is the way it is.

data.title: Summary
points: State the decision, constraints, and outcome clearly
Evaluate rejected alternatives with equal seriousness
Connect the architecture to team and business realities
Show that you would change the decision if the context changed
data.takeaway: A defended decision is not a fortress; it is a transparent explanation of why the choice made sense at the time and how you know when it is time to change.
